subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Vitamin K-dependent factors and natural anticoagulants
vignette: A newborn delivered at term did not receive vitamin K prophylaxis and develops bleeding in the first days of life. Neonates lack the enteric bacteria that synthesize vitamin K, leading to impaired gamma-carboxylation of several clotting factors. Which group of factors is vitamin K-dependent?
question: Vitamin K deficiency impairs maturation of which coagulation factors?

options.text: Factors II, VII, IX, X (plus proteins C and S)

explanation_correct: Vitamin K is required for gamma-carboxylation and maturation of factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as the natural anticoagulants proteins C and S. Neonates lack enteric bacteria that produce vitamin K, so prophylaxis is given to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn; broad-spectrum antibiotics that suppress gut flora can also contribute. Reduced carboxylation leaves these factors inactive.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factors I (fibrinogen), V, and VIII are not vitamin K-dependent; only factor II in this list is.
explanation_incorrect.B: Factors V, VIII, and XI are not vitamin K-dependent; only factor VII is.
explanation_incorrect.C: Factors VIII, XI, and XII are not vitamin K-dependent; only factor IX is.
explanation_incorrect.E: Factors I and V are not vitamin K-dependent, although II, VII, and X are.

educationalObjective: Vitamin K-dependent factors are II, VII, IX, X, plus proteins C and S.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Vitamin K-dependent factors and natural anticoagulants
vignette: A 67-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is started on an oral anticoagulant for stroke prevention. After several days his prothrombin time (INR) becomes elevated. The drug acts by inhibiting a hepatic enzyme that regenerates reduced vitamin K, preventing carboxylation of clotting factors. Which enzyme does this drug inhibit?
question: Warfarin exerts its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting which enzyme?
explanation_correct: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of reduced (active) vitamin K and thereby decreasing gamma-carboxylation and maturation of factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S. Vitamin K administration can reverse warfarin's effect but only in a delayed fashion because new factors must be synthesized; for immediate reversal in severe bleeding, FFP or PCC is given, often with vitamin K.

explanation_incorrect.B: Cyclooxygenase-1 is the enzyme inhibited by aspirin, not warfarin.
explanation_incorrect.C: Antithrombin III is enhanced by heparin; warfarin does not act through antithrombin.
explanation_incorrect.D: Warfarin does not directly inhibit the carboxylase; it acts upstream by blocking regeneration of reduced vitamin K via epoxide reductase.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tissue plasminogen activator is a thrombolytic and is not involved in warfarin's mechanism.

educationalObjective: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, producing inactive under-carboxylated clotting factors.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Vitamin K-dependent factors and natural anticoagulants
vignette: A patient with a proximal deep vein thrombosis is treated with intravenous heparin, which acts by markedly enhancing the activity of a circulating serine protease inhibitor. This inhibitor blocks several activated coagulation factors, with its principal physiologic targets being thrombin and factor Xa. Which endogenous anticoagulant does heparin enhance?
question: Heparin accelerates the activity of which endogenous anticoagulant?
explanation_correct: Antithrombin (antithrombin III) inhibits thrombin (factor IIa) and factors VIIa, IXa, Xa, XIa, and XIIa, with thrombin and factor Xa as its principal targets. Heparin, including low-molecular-weight heparin, greatly enhances antithrombin's activity and produces rapid anticoagulation. This is distinct from the vitamin K-dependent protein C/protein S system and from factor V Leiden, which confers resistance to activated protein C.

explanation_incorrect.A: Protein C, with protein S, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa; it is vitamin K-dependent and is not enhanced by heparin.
explanation_incorrect.C: Protein S is a cofactor for activated protein C; heparin does not act through it.
explanation_incorrect.D: C1-inhibitor restrains the kallikrein/contact and complement pathways; its deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor inhibits the tissue factor-VIIa complex; it is not the target enhanced by heparin.

educationalObjective: Heparin enhances antithrombin, whose main targets are thrombin (IIa) and factor Xa.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Vitamin K-dependent factors and natural anticoagulants
vignette: A 34-year-old woman with no prior medical problems develops a second episode of unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. Testing shows that her factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, even though protein C and protein S levels are normal. Which inherited thrombophilia is most likely?
question: Factor V resistance to activated protein C is the hallmark of which thrombophilia?
explanation_correct: Factor V Leiden is a point mutation that makes factor V resistant to cleavage and inactivation by activated protein C, leading to persistent factor Va activity and a hypercoagulable state. It is the most common inherited thrombophilia and must be distinguished from deficiencies of protein C, protein S, or antithrombin, which are separate mechanisms. The protein C/protein S system itself is vitamin K-dependent.

explanation_incorrect.A: Protein C deficiency reduces activated protein C levels, but factor V remains normally sensitive to it; it is a different inherited thrombophilia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Protein S deficiency impairs the cofactor for activated protein C, but factor V itself is not resistant.
explanation_incorrect.C: Antithrombin deficiency reduces inhibition of thrombin and Xa; it does not involve the protein C pathway.
explanation_incorrect.D: Prothrombin gene mutation increases prothrombin (factor II) levels and does not cause activated protein C resistance.

educationalObjective: Factor V Leiden is factor V resistant to activated protein C and causes inherited thrombophilia.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
subtopic: Vitamin K-dependent factors and natural anticoagulants
vignette: A patient starting warfarin needs monitoring because the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors have very different half-lives. The anticoagulant effect on these factors appears at different rates, with the shortest-lived factor falling first. Which vitamin K-dependent factor has the shortest half-life?
question: Which vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor has the shortest half-life?
explanation_correct: Factor VII has the shortest half-life among the vitamin K-dependent factors, so its level falls first after warfarin is started and the PT rises early. Factor II (prothrombin) has the longest half-life, which is why full anticoagulation takes several days and why factor II takes longest to replace. This difference is clinically important when managing warfarin initiation or reversal.

explanation_incorrect.A: Factor II (prothrombin) has the longest, not the shortest, half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Factor IX is vitamin K-dependent but has an intermediate half-life, longer than that of factor VII.
explanation_incorrect.D: Factor X is vitamin K-dependent but does not have the shortest half-life.
explanation_incorrect.E: Protein C is vitamin K-dependent, but factor VII has the shortest half-life.

educationalObjective: Factor VII has the shortest half-life; factor II has the longest half-life among vitamin K-dependent factors.
